title: Does Reasoning Improve Seeing? Understanding When Vision-Language Models Benefit from Thinking
claim: Easy inputs engage perception-oriented components while hard inputs recruit reasoning-oriented components, so computation should adapt to task difficulty.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, top-to-bottom; image and question above stacked colored head blocks
description: Two side-by-side panels compare an easy question and a hard question. Each panel has a bold serif title and a gray-bordered photo of a white fluffy dog with a question caption underneath. The left panel shows a dog lying down and asks 'What is the color of the dog?'. The right panel shows a dog with its tongue out wearing a tan harness and asks 'What does the facial expression mean?'. Below each photo is a staggered grid of colored squares standing for attention heads, in gray, blue, teal, yellow, green and orange. On the left the bottom row is yellow and green, labeled 'Perception heads activated'. On the right the bottom row is green and orange, labeled 'Reasoning heads activated'. The eye goes first to the dog photos, then to the colored head blocks.
caption: Difficulty-dependent head activation. Easy questions
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) now support both direct Instruct and explicit-reasoning Thinking modes, yet practitioners still lack principled ways to decide when reasoning actually improves performance, or how much computation to spend at test time, so we investigate whether VLMs encode meta-cognitive signals for adaptive inference. We derive oracle labels for two properties: (1) reasoning helpfulness, namely whether explicit reasoning improves accuracy, and (2) desired generation length, the minimal token budget needed for a correct answer. Probing final-layer representations in InternVL and Qwen3-VL models, we find Thinking models encode these signals more linearly than Instruct models, suggesting that reasoning-oriented training enhances meta-cognitive structure. Head-wise attribution reveals two circuits: length-control heads in lower layers and reasoning/difficulty heads in higher layers. Causal interventions confirm these roles across benchmarks: scaling length heads controls output length with minimal accuracy loss, while scaling reasoning heads enables a perception-reasoning trade-off, improving accuracy by up to 5.3\%. Our results demonstrate that reasoning-tuned VLMs develop localized, manipulable circuits for meta-cognitive control, enabling test-time steering of computation and reasoning without retraining.
